prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The case rests on a rare, complete chain from basic physiology (Holst on secretion and action in humans, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology, Mojsov on the active GLP-1(7-36) form) to therapies with large, independently confirmed effects on glycaemia, body weight and, in outcome trials, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. The mechanism is mature, replicated, and the impact is global. A citation anchored on the physiological discoveries and the active peptide keeps the prize on discovery rather than on a single commercial product.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the weak point. Habener's contribution is absent from the supplied names, priority over identification of the active peptide is disputed, and Lotte Bjerre Knudsen's peptide-engineering work for liraglutide and semaglutide is excluded by the three-laureate cap. A prize that omits the drug developers risks being read as recognising only the upstream discovery, while one that includes them risks diluting the physiological core. I have not independently verified the priority claims and would want the dossier checked before the final ballot.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked TOR signalling second, with Hall as the decisive conceptual figure and Schreiber supplying the rapamycin-FKBP12 chemical entry point, while hesitating over Sabatini.
responses.response: I agree that Hall is the central name and that the discovery is fundamental, and I share the hesitation about Sabatini. My reservation is about the clinical payoff. Rapalogs are established in transplantation and some oncology, but the broader therapeutic promise of mTOR modulation is still emerging, and the Hall-Schreiber pair leaves out earlier rapamycin work such as Heitman and Sehgal. I therefore keep TOR below the leading candidates. I do not see it competing with GLP-1 for the prize this year, and I could accept it as a later candidate if the allocation becomes cleaner.

responses.point: Perlmann proposed only June and Sadelain for CAR-T, treating Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer and TIL work as foundational to cell therapy but separable from CAR engineering.
responses.response: I think this is the sharper reading and I move toward it. Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a broader achievement, and including him forces a citation that blends cell therapy with CAR design. A June-Sadelain citation on the design and clinical proof of CAR T cells is more coherent, although it still leaves Eshhar's first-generation chimeric receptor concept outside the credit. That omission is serious enough that I would hold CAR-T as my first alternative rather than a co-prize with GLP-1.

responses.point: Sandberg proposed the GLP-1 trio but flagged that Knudsen's drug-development work is more naturally recognised separately, and that Mojsov's peptide chemistry contribution is contested yet substantial.
responses.response: I agree that Mojsov belongs in the trio because the active peptide identification is what made therapeutic design possible, and I agree that a discovery-only configuration is cleaner. I would qualify the idea that Knudsen can be recognised separately. Nobel practice rarely offers a second chance, so excluding her is a real cost, and I do not want the committee to treat it as costless. Even so, the three-name cap and the physiological framing favour Drucker, Holst and Mojsov.

responses.point: El Manira ranked optogenetics third and the unfolded protein response seventh, and noted that the GLP-1 allocation depends on whether the prize centres on the peptide or on drug development.
responses.response: I rank the UPR (Mori and Walter) above optogenetics, because its attribution is a clean two-person pair and the mechanism is a new principle of signalling, whereas six credited names for optogenetics cannot be reduced to three without omitting a decisive contributor. I accept your point that the UPR's medical impact is indirect, and that is why I place both behind GLP-1 and CAR-T. On the peptide-versus-drug question, I favour the peptide and physiology.

uncertainties: Whether Habener's absence from the credited names undermines a Drucker-Holst-Mojsov trio.
Whether excluding Knudsen is acceptable to the committee, or whether a second part for drug development should be considered.
Priority for the identification of the active GLP-1 peptide and my own recollection of chronology, which I have not verified.
How the committee weighs indirect medical impact (UPR, TOR) against therapeutic impact (CAR-T, BCR-ABL inhibition) if GLP-1 is settled.
statement.conflict_note: I co-authored the 2016 Science spatial transcriptomics paper and have eight recorded co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg (count not audited). None of the shortlisted candidates involves that work or any known collaboration, so no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
